title: Frobenius and factorization modulo primes
subject: galois
summary: Squarefree factorization modulo a prime determines a cycle type in the Galois group. Group-theoretic criteria then convert these cycle types into group containments.
questionsAnswered: What does a squarefree reduction say about the Galois group?
When can irreducibility be witnessed by one prime?
How do two primes prove that a quintic has group S5?

sections.title: The Dedekind–Frobenius theorem
sections.body:
Theorem · Dedekind–Frobenius

Let \(f\in\mathbb Z[x]\) be monic and separable, and let \(G\) be the Galois group of its splitting field over \(\mathbb Q\), acting on its \(n\) roots. If \(p\nmid\operatorname{disc}(f)\) and

\[\bar f=f_1\cdots f_r\quad\text{in }\mathbb F_p[x]\]

is its factorization into distinct monic irreducibles, then \(G\) contains a permutation whose cycle lengths are \(\deg f_1,\ldots,\deg f_r\).

The cycle statement does not require irreducibility of \(f\). Irreducibility is the additional condition that makes \(G\) transitive. For nonmonic integral polynomials, also exclude primes dividing the leading coefficient.

citations.note: The note treats irreducible monic polynomials; the same reduction argument gives the separable form stated here.

sections.title: Frobenius orbits
sections.body:
Choose a prime \(\mathfrak p\) of the splitting field above \(p\). The discriminant condition ensures that the roots remain distinct after reduction. Frobenius acts on the residue field by \(z\mapsto z^p\). A root of an irreducible degree-\(d\) factor has an orbit of length exactly \(d\) under this map. Lifting that action to the roots gives the required permutation.

A different choice of \(\mathfrak p\) conjugates Frobenius. Thus factorization determines the cycle type. It does not identify the root labels, so permutations obtained from different primes have no specified common labeling.

sections.title: Example
sections.body:
Example: \(S_5\)

Take \(f=x^5-x-1\). Modulo \(3\), it has no root. The only monic irreducible quadratics over \(\mathbb F_3\) are

\[x^2+1,\quad x^2+x+2,\quad x^2+2x+2.\]

The remainders on division of \(f\) by these are \(-1,x-1,x-1\), respectively. Every reducible quintic has a factor of degree at most two, so \(\bar f\) is irreducible over \(\mathbb F_3\). Hence \(f\) is irreducible over \(\mathbb Q\), and its group contains a 5-cycle.

Modulo \(2\),

\[f=(x^2+x+1)(x^3+x^2+1),\]

with distinct irreducible factors. This gives an element of type \((2,3)\), whose cube is a transposition.

A transitive action of prime degree is primitive. A primitive group containing a transposition is the full symmetric group, as proved in the permutation-group entry. Therefore \(\operatorname{Gal}(f/\mathbb Q)=S_5\).

citations.note: Recognition criterion used after the explicit finite-field computations.
Classical irreducibility of the broader trinomial family; the present degree-five proof is self-contained.

sections.title: Chebotarev density
sections.body:
By Chebotarev, every conjugacy class of \(G\) occurs at infinitely many unramified primes. The density for a class \(C\) is \(|C|/|G|\); a cycle type may comprise several classes of \(G\), in which case their densities add.

Consequently, an irreducible polynomial of degree \(n\) has an irreducible reduction at some good prime if and only if \(G\) contains an \(n\)-cycle. Transitivity alone does not guarantee this. For \(x^4+1\), the group is the Klein four-group and no good prime yields an irreducible quartic reduction.

citations.note: Chebotarev density and Frobenius interpretation.

sections.title: Limits of modular tests
sections.body:
Remark

The theorem requires squarefree reduction. Failure to observe a cycle type in a finite search does not exclude it. A finite list of factorizations determines the group only if a recognition theorem or a complete subgroup analysis excludes every other compatible group.

At primes of repeated reduction, ramification and Newton polygons may give further permutations. Resolvents can distinguish groups with the same observed cycle types.

related.why: Permutation-group criteria determine which groups contain the observed cycle types.
The discriminant identifies good primes and the parity character.
Ramification and Newton polygons apply at primes where reduction is not squarefree.
Modular factorizations restrict the candidate groups in an exact computation.

questions.title: Does every irreducible rational polynomial remain irreducible modulo some prime?
questions.body: No. Such a reduction exists precisely when the Galois group contains a full cycle. The polynomial \(x^4+1\) is a counterexample.

title: Discriminants, parity, and ramification
subject: galois
summary: The discriminant vanishes precisely when roots repeat. For a separable polynomial in characteristic different from two, its square class determines the sign character of the Galois group.
questionsAnswered: Why does a square discriminant put the group inside A_n?
What distinguishes polynomial and number-field discriminants?
When does parity finish a Galois-group proof?

sections.title: Definition
sections.body:
For \(f(x)=a_n\prod_{i=1}^n(x-\alpha_i)\) of degree \(n\), the polynomial discriminant is

\[\Delta(f)=a_n^{2n-2}\prod_{i\lt j}(\alpha_i-\alpha_j)^2=(-1)^{n(n-1)/2}a_n^{-1}\operatorname{Res}(f,f').\]

It is nonzero exactly when the roots are distinct. The resultant formula computes it from coefficients without computing the roots. Multiplying \(f\) by a nonzero scalar changes its discriminant by an even power, so its square class is unchanged.

citations.locator: Chapter 4 and its appendix on resultants

sections.title: The discriminant criterion
sections.body:
Theorem · discriminant criterion

If \(f\in K[x]\) is separable and \(\operatorname{char}K\ne2\), then

\[\operatorname{Gal}(f/K)\subseteq A_n\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\Delta(f)\in K^{\times2}.\]

Proof

Set \(D=a_n^{n-1}\prod_{i\lt j}(\alpha_i-\alpha_j)\), so \(D^2=\Delta(f)\). An automorphism \(\sigma\) sends \(D\) to \(\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)D\). Thus all automorphisms are even exactly when \(D\) belongs to the ground field. Conversely, if \(D^2=b^2\) with \(b\in K\), then \(D=\pm b\), so \(D\in K\). Characteristic two is excluded because the signs coincide.

If the group is not contained in \(A_n\), the quadratic field \(K(\sqrt{\Delta(f)})\) is the fixed field of the kernel of the sign character.

citations.locator: Chapter 4, “When is G_f contained in A_n?”

sections.title: Cubics
sections.body:
Example

A separable irreducible cubic has a transitive subgroup of \(S_3\), hence group \(A_3\) or \(S_3\). For \(x^3+ax+b\), the discriminant is \(-4a^3-27b^2\). Therefore

\[\begin{array}{c|c|c} f & \Delta(f) & \operatorname{Gal}(f/\mathbb Q)\\ \hline x^3-x-1&-23&S_3\\ x^3-3x-1&81&C_3\end{array}\]

The rational-root test proves both polynomials irreducible: neither \(1\) nor \(-1\) is a root. Irreducibility is required to apply the cubic classification.

sections.title: Quartic examples
sections.body:
The polynomial \(x^4+1\) is irreducible over \(\mathbb Q\), since replacing \(x\) by \(x+1\) makes it Eisenstein at \(2\). Its discriminant is \(256\), but its splitting field is \(\mathbb Q(\zeta_8)\), whose group is \((\mathbb Z/8\mathbb Z)^\times\simeq C_2\times C_2\), strictly smaller than \(A_4\).

For a nonsquare example, \(x^4-2\) is Eisenstein at \(2\) and has nonsquare discriminant \(-2048\). Its splitting field is \(\mathbb Q(\sqrt[4]{2},i)\), of degree eight: the real field \(\mathbb Q(\sqrt[4]{2})\) has degree four and does not contain \(i\). The group is dihedral of order eight, not \(S_4\).

Remark

If \(A_n\subseteq G\) is known, a square discriminant gives \(G=A_n\), and a nonsquare discriminant gives \(G=S_n\). The containment is essential.

citations.note: Cyclotomic and radical extensions; discriminant interpretation.

sections.title: Polynomial and field discriminants
sections.body:
If \(f\) is the monic minimal polynomial of an algebraic integer \(\alpha\), and \(K=\mathbb Q(\alpha)\), then

\[\Delta(f)=\operatorname{disc}(K)\,[\mathcal O_K:\mathbb Z[\alpha]]^2.\]

The two discriminants have the same square class, but can have different prime divisors. A prime dividing \(\Delta(f)\) may come from the index rather than ramification in \(K\).

For \(f=x^2-5\), the polynomial discriminant is \(20\), whereas \(\operatorname{disc}(\mathbb Q(\sqrt5))=5\). Reduction modulo \(2\) is repeated, although \(2\) is unramified in the quadratic field. The integral generator \((1+\sqrt5)/2\), with polynomial \(x^2-x-1\), removes this index obstruction.

Over \(\mathbb Q\), complex conjugation also determines the sign of the discriminant: with \(r\) nonreal conjugate pairs it has type \(2^r1^{n-2r}\), and \(\operatorname{sgn}\Delta(f)=(-1)^r\).

citations.note: Discriminants of orders, indices, and ramification.

questions.title: When can a discriminant determine the full Galois group?
questions.scope: Separable irreducible cubics; groups already known to contain \(A_n\).
questions.body: It determines the group for irreducible cubics, and whenever an independent argument has proved \(A_n\subseteq G\). In general it determines only whether \(G\subseteq A_n\).

title: Transitivity, primitivity, and cycle criteria
subject: galois
summary: Blocks, transpositions, and long cycles give criteria for alternating-group containment and equality with the symmetric group.
questionsAnswered: How can primitivity be proved?
Why does a primitive group with a transposition equal S_n?
Which single cycles force containment of A_n?

sections.title: Blocks and primitivity
sections.body:
Let \(G\le S_n\) act on \(\Omega\). A nonempty subset \(B\subseteq\Omega\) is a block if each translate \(gB\) is either equal to \(B\) or disjoint from it. A transitive action is primitive if its only blocks have size \(1\) or \(n\).

In a transitive action, translates of a block partition \(\Omega\) into subsets of equal size. Hence a transitive action of prime degree is primitive. For an irreducible separable polynomial with root \(\alpha\), the action is primitive exactly when the root field \(K(\alpha)\) has no proper intermediate field between \(K\) and \(K(\alpha)\). This follows by applying the Galois correspondence to subgroups between a root stabilizer and the whole group.

For a polynomial map, decomposition of \(f(X)\) is related to primitivity of the monodromy action of \(f(X)-t\) over a function field. This is a different action from the Galois action on the roots of a fixed polynomial.

citations.note: Blocks, stabilizers, and primitive actions.
Galois correspondence and the action on conjugates.

sections.title: Transpositions
sections.body:
Theorem

A primitive subgroup \(G\le S_n\) containing a transposition is \(S_n\).

Proof

Form a graph on \(\Omega\), joining \(a\) to \(b\) when \((a\ b)\in G\). Conjugation by \(G\) preserves this graph, so its connected components form a block system. There is an edge, and primitivity forces the graph to be connected. The transpositions associated with the edges of a connected graph generate every transposition: along a path, conjugating successive edge transpositions moves an endpoint step by step. They therefore generate \(S_n\), which is contained in \(G\).

Primitivity cannot be replaced by transitivity. The dihedral group \(\langle(1234),(13)\rangle\) has order eight and contains a transposition, while preserving the block system \(\{\{1,3\},\{2,4\}\}\). It is a proper subgroup of \(S_4\).

citations.note: Primitive permutation groups and generation by transpositions.
A useful sufficient condition for the required primitivity.

sections.title: Long prime cycles
sections.body:
Suppose \(G\) is transitive and contains a \(q\)-cycle, with \(q\) prime and \(q\gt n/2\). If a nontrivial block system had \(a\) blocks of size \(b\), then \(a,b\le n/2\lt q\). The cycle's induced action on the blocks has order dividing \(q\); since \(a\lt q\), it must fix every block. Its restriction to each block is also trivial because \(b\lt q\). This contradicts the presence of a \(q\)-cycle. Thus \(G\) is primitive.

Taking powers can isolate a cycle under a coprimality condition. If one cycle has length \(m\) coprime to every other cycle length, raising the permutation to the least common multiple of the other lengths eliminates those cycles and preserves an \(m\)-cycle. An element of type \((3,3)\) does not yield a single 3-cycle by this argument.

sections.title: Double transitivity
sections.body:
Theorem

For \(n\ge3\), a transitive subgroup \(G\le S_n\) containing an \((n-1)\)-cycle is doubly transitive. If it also contains a transposition, then \(G=S_n\).

Proof

If the cycle fixes \(a\), its powers act transitively on the other \(n-1\) points. Thus the stabilizer \(G_a\) is transitive there. Transitivity of \(G\) now moves any ordered pair of distinct points to any other: first move the first point, then use its stabilizer to move the second. This is double transitivity. Conjugating one transposition by these elements supplies every transposition, which generates \(S_n\).

No primality condition on \(n-1\) is needed. In arithmetic applications, a good reduction of factor degrees \((1,n-1)\) supplies the long cycle. Irreducibility supplies transitivity. A second squarefree pattern with one 2-cycle and all other cycles of odd lengths supplies a transposition by taking an odd power. These conditions depend only on cycle types and therefore require no common labeling of roots across primes.

citations.note: The stabilizer characterization of double transitivity; the short proof is included here.
Arithmetic cycle-type witnesses and extracting a transposition by taking a power.

sections.title: Jordan's theorem and Jones's extension
sections.body:
Theorem (Jordan)

If a primitive subgroup \(G\le S_n\) contains a \(q\)-cycle with \(q\) prime and \(q\le n-3\), then \(A_n\subseteq G\).

Combining this with the preceding argument gives the following criterion: transitivity plus a prime cycle with \(n/2\lt q\le n-3\) forces \(A_n\). Newton polygons often produce just such a prime divisor of the group order; the inequality \(q\gt n/2\) ensures an element of order \(q\) is one cycle.

Theorem (Jones)

A primitive subgroup containing a nontrivial single cycle that fixes at least three points contains \(A_n\). The cycle length need not be prime.

This stronger result follows from the classification in Jones's paper and uses the classification of finite simple groups. The classical prime-cycle theorem does not require that classification. Both theorems assume primitivity.

citations.note: Historical source for primitive-group criteria.

sections.title: Example
sections.body:
Example · \(x^5-4x+2\)

This polynomial is Eisenstein at \(2\), hence irreducible. Its action has prime degree five and is primitive. Put \(a=(4/5)^{1/4}\). The derivative \(5x^4-4\) vanishes only at \(-a,a\); the local maximum has value \(2+16a/5\gt 0\), and the local minimum has value \(2-16a/5\lt 0\), since \(a\gt 5/8\). Monotonicity on the three intervals gives exactly three real roots.

The remaining two roots form one nonreal conjugate pair. Complex conjugation is therefore a transposition. The transposition criterion proves \(\operatorname{Gal}(x^5-4x+2\,/\mathbb Q)=S_5\).

citations.locator: Chapter 4, “Examples of polynomials with S_p as Galois group over Q”

related.why: Suitable Newton-slope denominators force long prime cycles.

Polynomial decomposition concerns function-field monodromy; primitivity of a root action concerns intermediate fields.
Inverse pairs form blocks for the Galois action.

questions.title: Can the prime-length assumption in Jordan’s cycle criterion be removed?
questions.scope: Primitive finite permutation groups containing a nontrivial cycle with at least three fixed points

title: Resolvents and subgroup tests
subject: galois
summary: Resolvent factorization describes Galois orbits of expressions in the roots. A simple rational root detects containment in a conjugate of the corresponding stabilizer.
field: Q; fields of characteristic not 2 for quartics
questionsAnswered: How does a polynomial in the roots detect a subgroup?
How is the cubic resolvent of a quartic constructed?
What distinguishes S4, A4, V4, and the C4/D4 cases?

sections.title: Invariant polynomials and coset actions
sections.body:
Let \(f\in K[x]\) be separable, with roots \(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_n\); suppose its Galois group is contained in \(G_0\le S_n\). Choose \(\Phi\in K[X_1,\ldots,X_n]\) with formal stabilizer \(H\) in \(G_0\). Evaluate its orbit to obtain values \(\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_m\), where \(m=[G_0:H]\), and form

\[R_\Phi(T)=\prod_{j=1}^m(T-\beta_j).\]

The actual Galois group permutes these values, so \(R_\Phi\) has coefficients in the ground field. If the values are distinct, its irreducible factor degrees are the orbit sizes for this new action. A root in the ground field gives a fixed coset, hence containment of the Galois group in a conjugate of \(H\).

Distinctness is essential: equal evaluated invariants can otherwise give a false subgroup containment. A nonzero resolvent discriminant certifies distinctness; if it vanishes, different root expressions may be needed.

citations.note: The subgroup-descent principle.

sections.title: The cubic resolvent
sections.body:
For \(f=x^4+ax^3+bx^2+cx+d\), the three partitions of its four roots into two unordered pairs give

\[\beta_1=\alpha_1\alpha_2+\alpha_3\alpha_4,\quad\beta_2=\alpha_1\alpha_3+\alpha_2\alpha_4,\quad\beta_3=\alpha_1\alpha_4+\alpha_2\alpha_3.\]

Expanding \(\prod(T-\beta_i)\) in elementary symmetric functions yields

\[R_f(T)=T^3-bT^2+(ac-4d)T+4bd-a^2d-c^2.\]

The action \(S_4\to S_3\) on the three pairings has kernel the normal Klein four-group. Moreover, \(\beta_1-\beta_2=(\alpha_1-\alpha_4)(\alpha_2-\alpha_3)\), with analogous formulas for the other differences. Their squared product proves \(\operatorname{disc}(R_f)=\operatorname{disc}(f)\), so this resolvent is separable whenever \(f\) is.

citations.note: Resolvents and their relation to permutation actions.

sections.title: Quartic Galois groups
sections.body:
Assume \(\operatorname{char}K\ne2\) and \(f\) is a separable irreducible quartic over \(K\). Then:

Resolvent over \(K\)Discriminant of \(f\)Galois group
IrreducibleNonsquare\(S_4\)
IrreducibleSquare\(A_4\)
Splits completelySquare\(V_4\)
One linear factor and one irreducible quadraticNonsquare\(C_4\) or \(D_4\)

Here \(D_4\) denotes the dihedral group of order eight. The last row requires an additional test. If \(r\in K\) is the unique root of \(R_f\), they are separated by the following test: the group is \(C_4\) precisely when both \(T^2+aT+(b-r)\) and \(T^2-rT+d\) split over \(K(\sqrt{\Delta(f)})\); otherwise it is \(D_4\).

citations.note: Original published quartic-group test; Conrad Theorem 4.1 gives the exact formulation used here.

sections.title: Example
sections.body:
Example · \(f=x^4+2x+2\)

Eisenstein at \(2\) proves irreducibility. The resolvent is \(R_f=T^3-8T-4\). By the rational-root test a rational root would be one of \(\pm1,\pm2,\pm4\); the six values, in the order \(-4,-2,-1,1,2,4\), are \(-36,4,3,-11,-12,28\). None is zero, so \(R_f\) is irreducible.

The discriminant is

\[256\cdot2^3-27\cdot2^4=1616=16\cdot101.\]

It is nonsquare. The first line of the classification gives \(\operatorname{Gal}(f/\mathbb Q)=S_4\).

citations.note: The example also appears in the source; the arithmetic is displayed here in full.

sections.title: Cyclic and dihedral examples
sections.body:
Example (cyclic group)

For \(f=x^4+x^3+x^2+x+1\), translation gives \(f(x+1)=x^4+5x^3+10x^2+10x+5\), which is Eisenstein at \(5\). Here

\[\Delta(f)=125,\qquad R_f(T)=(T-2)(T^2+T-1).\]

The unique rational resolvent root is \(r=2\), and the discriminant field is \(\mathbb Q(\sqrt5)\). The two test polynomials are \(T^2+T-1\) and \((T-1)^2\). Both split over that field, so the group is \(C_4\).

Example (dihedral group)

For \(f=x^4-2\), Eisenstein at \(2\) proves irreducibility. Now

\[\Delta(f)=-2048,\qquad R_f(T)=T(T^2+8).\]

Thus \(r=0\), the discriminant field is \(\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-2})\), and the test polynomials are \(T^2\) and \(T^2-2\). The latter does not split there: a real element of this imaginary quadratic field is rational, while \(\sqrt2\) is not. Hence the group is \(D_4\), of order eight.

Both resolvents have the same factor degrees \((1,2)\). The extra quadratic-field test distinguishes their groups.

citations.note: Original group-separation method.
Exact test used in these independently calculated examples.

sections.title: Relative resolvents
sections.body:
Factorization modulo a good prime determines a cycle type. Resolvent factorization describes orbits in another permutation action. The two tests give complementary restrictions; a rational resolvent root can identify a preserved partition that the observed cycle types do not determine.

In larger degrees, an absolute resolvent can be expensive to compute. Stauduhar's method descends through successive subgroup candidates using relative invariants. Fieker and Klüners explain how to construct invariants from group structure and how to certify the relevant factors. A numerical approximation to an integer must be verified before it can certify a factorization.

related.why: The discriminant distinguishes the alternating and symmetric cases in the quartic classification.

title: Polynomial factorization algorithms
subject: algorithms
summary: Finite-field factorization uses Frobenius maps and linear algebra. Factorization over the rationals combines modular factorization, Hensel lifting, and lattice reduction.
field: Finite fields, Q, and p-adic fields
questionsAnswered: Which methods underlie exact polynomial factorization?
Why is modular factorization followed by recombination?
How can a randomized computation still produce exact factors?
How do recent modular-composition advances relate to factorization?
How are local factors found when reduction has repeated factors?

sections.title: Finite-field factorization
sections.body:
Let the polynomial have coefficients in \(\mathbb F_q\). A squarefree decomposition separates repeated factors, using gcds with the derivative. If the derivative vanishes, the polynomial is a \(p\)-th power over the finite field and one first takes its \(p\)-th root.

For a squarefree polynomial, \(\gcd(f,x^{q^d}-x)\) selects its irreducible factors whose degrees divide \(d\). Removing the factors already found and repeating the gcd calculation gives a distinct-degree decomposition. Equal-degree splitting then separates factors of the same degree. Cantor–Zassenhaus uses random choices for this splitting step; the output consists of exact polynomial factors whose product and irreducibility can be checked.

citations.note: Squarefree, distinct-degree, and equal-degree factorization.

sections.title: Berlekamp's algorithm
sections.body:
Proposition

If \(f\) is squarefree with \(r\) distinct irreducible factors, then

\[\dim_{\mathbb F_q}\{h\in\mathbb F_q[x]/(f):h^q=h\}=r.\]

Indeed, the Chinese remainder theorem identifies the quotient with a product \(\prod_{i=1}^r\mathbb F_{q^{d_i}}\). The fixed elements of Frobenius on each component are exactly \(\mathbb F_q\). Finding the fixed subspace is linear algebra. A fixed element assumes constant values on the components; gcds \(\gcd(f,h-c)\), for \(c\in\mathbb F_q\), separate components with different values.

Example

Over \(\mathbb F_2\), take \(f=x^4+x\). Since \(f'=1\), it is squarefree. In the quotient, \(x^4=x\), and solving \(h^2=h\) gives the basis \(1,x^2+x,x^3\). Thus there are three irreducible factors. The gcds from \(h=x^3\) first split off \(x\); those from \(h=x^2+x\) split the remaining cubic. The result is

\[x^4+x=x(x+1)(x^2+x+1).\]

The quadratic has no root in \(\mathbb F_2\), which completes the factorization.

citations.note: Frobenius-fixed algebra and the linear-algebra factorization method.

sections.title: Modular composition
sections.body:
The operation modular composition takes \(a,g,f\in K[x]\), with \(f\) monic of degree \(n\) and \(\deg a,\deg g<n\), and computes \(g(a(x))\bmod f(x)\). It avoids storing a composition whose unreduced degree can be nearly \(n^2\).

Frobenius as modular composition

In \(A=\mathbb F_q[x]/(f)\), put \(a=x^q\bmod f\). For every \(h\in\mathbb F_q[x]\),

\[h(x)^q\equiv h(a(x))\pmod f.\]

The coefficients are fixed by the \(q\)-power map. Thus one application of Frobenius is a modular composition. Iterates of this map supply the powers used in distinct-degree factorization and irreducibility tests.

Example

Over \(\mathbb F_2\), take \(f=x^3+x+1\). Since \(x^3=x+1\) in the quotient, applying Frobenius to \(h=x^2+x\) gives

\[h^2=x^4+x^2=(x^2+x)+x^2=x.\]

Equivalently, compose \(h\) with \(a=x^2\) and reduce modulo \(f\).

Brent–Kung's baby-step/giant-step method groups powers of \(a\) into blocks and combines them by matrix multiplication. Later methods encode small algebraic relations between \(x\) and \(a\) in polynomial matrices, or reduce the task to multivariate evaluation. Both approaches avoid forming the full intermediate composition.

citations.locator: Composition algorithms; see also Neiger–Salvy–Schost–Villard (2024), Section 1.1, for modular composition

sections.title: Complexity bounds
sections.body:
A field-operation count charges unit cost for arithmetic in \(K\). A bit-operation count includes the representation and size of coefficients. Over \(\mathbb F_q\), these are not interchangeable uniformly in \(q\). Modular composition is one step of a factorization algorithm.

SourcePrecise scopeContribution
Kedlaya–Umans (2011)Modular composition over \(\mathbb F_q\); bit complexityFor each fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), \(n^{1+\varepsilon}\log^{1+o(1)}q\) bit operations in sufficiently large degree. This leads to a randomized finite-field factorization bound, displayed below.
Neiger–Salvy–Schost–Villard (2024)Arbitrary fields of known characteristic; arithmetic complexityA Las Vegas method with expected \(O(n^{1.43})\) field operations. Small finite fields are handled through a suitably enlarged extension; a failed randomized trial is detected.
Neiger–Salvy–Schost–Villard (2026)Fixed \(f\), generic inner polynomial \(a\); arithmetic complexityTwo relation matrices give \(\widetilde O(n^{(\omega+3)/4})\) field operations. Here \(\omega\) is a feasible square-matrix multiplication exponent. The genericity requirement is essential.
van der Hoeven–Lecerf (2026)Modular composition over \(\mathbb Z/r\mathbb Z\); bit complexityA sharper nearly linear bound via spiroids and Fourier transforms with proved precision control. Prime finite fields are a special case.

The Kedlaya–Umans randomized factorization bound is

\[O\!\left(n^{3/2+o(1)}\log^{1+o(1)}q+n^{1+o(1)}\log^{2+o(1)}q\right).\]

A faster modular-composition subroutine does not by itself turn this exponent into \(1\). Guo–Narayanan–Umans (2016) organize related algebraic problems through reductions that would transfer an improvement below the factorization exponent \(3/2\). These reductions do not establish an optimal lower bound.

Conditional approach. Umans–Wang (2025) propose structured sets of integers with a divisibility-covering property as a route to faster factorization. Their proposed improvement depends on a number-theoretic conjecture; it is not an unconditional algorithm beating \(3/2\). The paper was listed for ISAAC in December 2026 when checked on 12 November; the reference below identifies the available preprint.

sections.title: Hensel lifting and recombination
sections.body:
Let \(f\in\mathbb Z[x]\) be monic and squarefree. Choose a prime where its reduction remains squarefree, factor there, and lift the pairwise coprime factors modulo \(p,p^2,p^4,\ldots\) by Hensel's lemma. Coprimality permits the correction equations to be solved at each stage.

A rational factor may be a product of several lifted factors. Recombination determines which products descend to \(\mathbb Z[x]\). Bounds for the coefficients of a genuine factor turn sufficiently accurate modular coefficients into unique candidate integers. Exact division then accepts or rejects a candidate.

Reducibility modulo \(p\) alone gives no rational factor, since the local factors need not descend separately. An irreducible good reduction, however, proves rational irreducibility immediately.

citations.note: Hensel lifting, coefficient bounds, and modular factorization.

sections.title: Local factorization and higher Newton polygons
sections.body:
Local factorization over \(\mathbb Q_p\) remains possible when every factor of \(\bar f\) is repeated. A residual polynomial separates roots that share a Newton slope; higher Newton polygons continue when that residual information is insufficient. The Montes method organizes successive slopes, residue-field extensions, and polynomial representatives into types. Complete types identify irreducible local factors and their ramification indices and residue degrees.

Guàrdia–Montes–Nart give the underlying theory and an algorithm for prime ideal decomposition and discriminants. Poteaux–Weimann's ISSAC 2022 paper improves local factorization through Hensel lifting adapted to these valuations and a divide-and-conquer strategy. Its sharper complexity bound assumes residue characteristic zero or greater than the polynomial degree; residual-field factorization costs are accounted for separately.

A local factor is represented to a stated \(p\)-adic precision together with exact structural data; its coefficients need not be rational. Recovering rational factors still requires global recombination and certification.

sections.title: Lattice reduction
sections.body:
The number of subsets of lifted factors is exponential in the number of factors. The Lenstra–Lenstra–Lovász theorem gives a deterministic algorithm for factoring rational polynomials in time polynomial in their degree and coefficient bit size, using lattice reduction. The lattice encodes congruence information; short vectors reveal relations compatible with a genuine factor.

Van Hoeij recasts practical recombination through a structured knapsack problem. Modern variants, including FLINT’s implementation, use logarithmic derivatives to turn products into sums, so a prospective factor corresponds to a vector of choices among local factors. Lattice reduction narrows the possible choice vectors before expensive exact tests. Belabas–van Hoeij–Klüners–Steel (2009) proved polynomial-time complexity for van Hoeij’s original rational-polynomial algorithm and natural variants. This recombination method uses local information to find exact global factors.

sections.title: Factorization certificates
sections.body:
The identity \(f=c\prod_i g_i^{e_i}\) proves a factorization, but not its completeness. Completeness additionally requires proof that each \(g_i\) is irreducible over the stated field. A modular irreducibility witness, a proved algorithm, or a suitable exact criterion can supply that step. A complete certificate specifies the coefficient field, normalization, multiplicities, and irreducibility proofs.

In a Las Vegas algorithm, random choices affect the runtime, while every returned factorization is correct. Numerical methods require exact verification before their output gives a factorization certificate.

questions.title: Is irreducibility over Q decidable in polynomial time?
questions.scope: Dense univariate polynomials given by rational coefficients in binary
questions.body: Yes. LLL gives polynomial-time factorization in the degree and coefficient bit size. The bound applies to dense binary input; it does not give the same complexity for every sparse encoding or extension-field representation.

questions.title: Can the 2026 generic composition bound be extended to arbitrary input?
questions.scope: Algebraic modular composition over a field; the two-relation-matrix method
questions.body: For each degree-\(n\) modulus \(f\), Theorem 1.3 supplies a nonempty Zariski-open set of coefficient vectors for \(a\) on which the faster bound holds. The algorithm can detect failure of its genericity conditions and fall back on another method. The authors explicitly leave a Las Vegas reduction for arbitrary input to future work. A nonempty Zariski-open set over an algebraic closure need not contain a point over a small finite base field; “generic” must not be silently replaced by “every.”

title: Algorithms for Galois groups
subject: algorithms
summary: Exact factorization, modular cycle types, and relative resolvents determine Galois groups. A certified computation records the permutation action and the data for its decisive tests.
field: Q, number fields, and p-adic fields
questionsAnswered: What data certify a computed Galois group?
How are resolvents combined with modular factorizations?
What are the software limits and certification requirements?

sections.title: Input and permutation action
sections.body:
The input is a polynomial and a ground field. For \(f\in\mathbb Q[x]\), clear denominators, remove content, and compute a squarefree factorization. A transitive-group label describes the action for an irreducible factor. If \(f\) is reducible, its whole splitting field is a compositum; the group need not be the direct product of the groups of the factors because their splitting fields can intersect.

For an irreducible degree-\(n\) input, the output should specify the subgroup of \(S_n\) up to conjugacy, together with its action on the roots. An abstract isomorphism type alone may lose information needed for cycle types, resolvents, subfields, or iteration.

sections.title: Subgroup descent
sections.body:
1. Irreducibility and separability. A factorization or irreducibility certificate establishes the input assumptions.
  2. Structural restrictions. The discriminant, reciprocity, composition, and known intermediate fields restrict the ambient permutation group.
  3. Local factorizations. Exact irreducible factorizations at good primes determine cycle types.
  4. Subgroup tests. Primitive-group theorems, relative resolvents, and subgroup descent eliminate incompatible candidates.
  5. Certification. The decisive tests require exact verification and retained proof data.

Stauduhar's method makes the fourth step systematic. Starting from a known overgroup, it tests relative invariants for maximal subgroups and descends whenever a certified resolvent condition permits it.

sections.title: Solvability by radicals
sections.body:
Landau–Miller (1985) give a polynomial-time decision procedure for solvability by radicals over \(\mathbb Q\), in the dense binary input model. Their paper also constructs radical expressions in a compact straight-line-program representation. The size bound applies to this compact encoding and need not survive expansion of repeated subexpressions.

The method exploits blocks of imprimitivity and the restricted size of primitive solvable permutation groups. Thus one can answer a structural question about a Galois group without first listing all its elements. This is different from constructing the splitting field in an explicit basis: its degree may be \(n!\) for a degree-\(n\) polynomial with group \(S_n\).

sections.title: Software
sections.body:
ToolScopeVerification data
MagmaNative GaloisGroup accepts integer, rational, and number-field polynomials without a fixed degree cap, but does not automatically prove its conditional steps. The documented GaloisProof(f,S) function covers integer polynomials; an absolute number-field overload is also available.Input, options, GaloisData, successful proof result, and version.
PARI/GP 2.19polgalois requires irreducible input over \(\mathbb Q\), of degree at most seven, or eleven with galdata. Its resolvent method can rarely return a wrong answer when initial numerical precision is insufficient.Polynomial, precision, complete output, numbering convention, and version.
SageMath 10.10The rational-polynomial galois_group interface requires irreducible input. It uses PARI through degree eleven and attempts GAP above that; GAP's documented algorithm range is through degree fifteen, with some higher cases possible. The Magma wrapper identifies groups only through degree thirty.Routine, algorithm, backend version, permutation action, and separate certification outcome.

Native Magma's degree-independent algorithm and Sage's wrapper have different limits. A database containing transitive groups of a given degree does not guarantee that the group-computation algorithm handles every polynomial of that degree. Runtime and memory can be decisive even without a formal degree cap.

For Sage number fields, gc_numbering controls whether permutations act on roots of the original defining polynomial or of the Galois closure's defining polynomial. The documentation also warns that calling galois_group on a relative extension currently computes its absolute Galois closure over \(\mathbb Q\); the intended ground field must therefore be specified explicitly.

Sage also documents galois_group_davenport_smith_test: return values \(1\) and \(2\) certify \(S_n\) and \(A_n\), while \(0\) means inconclusive. Its default checks irreducibility; setting assume_irreducible=True requires an independently established hypothesis. This specialized test is different from unrestricted group determination.

sections.title: Example
sections.body:
Example

For \(f=x^4+2x+2\), the following data determine the group:

  1. Eisenstein at \(2\), proving irreducibility.
  2. The resolvent \(R=T^3-8T-4\), with no rational root among \(\pm1,\pm2,\pm4\).
  3. The discriminant \(\Delta(f)=1616=16\cdot101\), a nonsquare.

The quartic classification proves the group is \(S_4\). The companion script verifies these identities and root tests by exact arithmetic.

A corresponding Magma command sequence is:

Zx<x> := PolynomialRing(Integers());
f := x^4 + 2*x + 2;
G, roots, S := GaloisGroup(f);
assert GaloisProof(f, S);
Order(G);

These commands are a template; no Magma execution is claimed here. The algebraic proof above establishes \(|G|=24\) without relying on that execution.

sections.title: Local Galois groups
sections.body:
For a rational polynomial, computing its group over \(\mathbb Q_p\) is distinct from computing its group over \(\mathbb Q\). If \(L/\mathbb Q\) is the global splitting field and \(\mathfrak P\mid p\), the local splitting-field group identifies with the decomposition subgroup \(D_{\mathfrak P}\subseteq\operatorname{Gal}(L/\mathbb Q)\). The embedding depends on the choice of \(\mathfrak P\), up to conjugacy.

Doris (2020) develops local algorithms using ramification towers, global models, and resolvents. A global model supplies a tractable overgroup; local factorization of resolvents distinguishes the desired subgroup. The base field therefore remains part of the result even when global auxiliary calculations are used.

Certification also depends on the implementation. Remark 3.5 of the paper identifies a heuristic complex-root bound in the then-current implementation. The author's package documentation later describes an exact \(p\)-adic input mode that produces proved results. The mode and verification outcome are part of the computation record; an algorithm does not by itself certify a finite-precision implementation.

citations.locator: Sections 1.1–4 and Remark 3.5; linked author package documentation for the exact-input mode

sections.title: Computations in families
sections.body:
A computation for a parameterized family specifies the parameter range, normalization, exceptions, and input polynomials. A finite verified range does not establish a result for all parameters; numerical experiments require a separate certification step.

Factor degrees usually identify the Frobenius cycle type rather than its precise conjugacy class in the group. Dokchitser and Dokchitser give finer invariants for distinguishing classes when cycle type is insufficient. This matters when arithmetic applications require more than the abstract group or its order.

A reproducible record includes exact coefficients, ground field, source theorem or algorithm, witness primes, discriminant, group action, certification outcome, and the date of the run. Databases supply comparison examples; the original computation or theorem supplies the proof.

questions.title: How can a computed group be certified?
questions.scope: Reproducible computations for explicit polynomial families
questions.body: Short certificates and verifiers for subgroup containment and noncontainment can simplify computations in a specified family. The quartic example illustrates such a certificate. The problem is to find suitable certificates for the chosen family, rather than to establish that Galois-group certification is possible.
